issues.claim: European 2023: REBOA may be considered as a bridge in noncompressible bleeding; ERC 2025 does not recommend REBOA outside clinical trials.
issues.problem: Confirmed. The REBOA point cites only European 2023 and ERC 2025. It leaves out EAST 2025, a GRADE guideline that conditionally recommends against REBOA in haemodynamically unstable trauma patients with suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding or suspected pelvic fracture; in pelvic fracture the pooled odds of death were twice as high with REBOA. The point offers 'may be considered' for exactly that population. The in-review Abdominal and pelvic trauma protocol (step 6 and its REBOA note) already reports EAST 2025, so the released protocol contradicts it. The source supports the in-review wording.
issues.correction: Replace with: 'REBOA — sources differ: European 2023 suggests considering it as a bridge in noncompressible life-threatening bleeding (2C); EAST 2025 conditionally recommends against it in unstable patients with suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding or pelvic fracture; ERC 2025 does not recommend it outside clinical trials.' Add cite(<EAST REBOA 2025>, "Table 1 — PICO 1 and 2"). The source tr-la-east-reboa-2025 is defined in the in-review TraumaLimbAbdomen.kt, so either move its definition into traumaSources or release both groups together; otherwise the integrity test (Sources.exists) will fail for the released group.
issues.evidence: EAST 2025 (Harfouche MN et al., Trauma Surg Acute Care Open 2025;10:e001730), Table 1 'Final committee recommendations for the use of REBOA': 'In hemodynamically unstable trauma patients with suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding, we conditionally recommend against using REBOA.' / 'In hemodynamically unstable trauma patients with suspected pelvic fractures, we conditionally recommend against using REBOA.' Recommendations—PICO 2: 'quantitative analysis demonstrated two times greater odds of mortality for the REBOA population.' https://doi.org/10.1136/tsaco-2024-001730 (full text PMC11956280)

issues.claim: REBOA: the European guideline 2023 suggests considering it for noncompressible bleeding as a bridge; ERC 2025 does not recommend it outside clinical trials.
issues.problem: The note leaves out EAST 2025, which addresses traumatic cardiac arrest directly. It conditionally recommends REBOA over resuscitative thoracotomy in traumatic cardiac arrest from suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding, and makes no recommendation for impending arrest. That is a third position that differs from ERC 2025's 'not outside trials', and the note does not report it.
issues.correction: Append to the note: 'EAST 2025 conditionally recommends REBOA over resuscitative thoracotomy in traumatic cardiac arrest from suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding (very low certainty), makes no recommendation for impending arrest, and requires that REBOA be part of a protocolised haemorrhage-control strategy with trained operators.' Add cite(<EAST REBOA 2025>, "Table 1 — PICO 3 and 4; Discussion"), with the same source-resolution step as the traumatic-haemorrhage issue.
issues.evidence: EAST 2025, Table 1: 'In trauma patients with cardiac arrest due to suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding, we conditionally recommend for using REBOA over RT.' / 'In trauma patients with cardiac arrest OR impending cardiac arrest due to suspected subdiaphragmatic bleeding, we cannot make a recommendation for or against using REBOA over RT.' Discussion: 'REBOA should not be used in isolation but should be part of a protocolized hemorrhage-control strategy. All providers using REBOA should be appropriately trained' — https://doi.org/10.1136/tsaco-2024-001730

issues.claim: Points cover documentation, hard signs, ABI, realignment, CT angiography, revascularisation within 1 h and fasciotomy. Citations: cite(LA_MOH, "Ch. 10 Major arterial haemorrhage (p. 48); ..."), cite(BOAST_ARTERIAL, "Standards 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15; footnote ii").
issues.problem: Nothing in the open-fracture protocol tells the doctor how to stop major bleeding from the limb, although all three Indian and BOA sources it cites give this first. The step cites MoHFW 'Major arterial haemorrhage (p. 48)' but leaves out MoHFW's stepwise control (pressure, then pressure dressing, then proximal arterial occlusion, then tourniquet). It cites BOAST 2026 but skips Standards 2–3 (immediate control by pressure, packing or tourniquet; no blind clamping; operate and resuscitate together if unstable). ICMR STW 2024's 'obvious bleed' arm (local pressure, then pack the wound) is also missing. No point refers to the Major trauma <C> step. In a limb-threatening vascular injury, bleeding control comes before everything this step lists.
issues.correction: Add as the first point: 'Bleeding — BOAST 2026: control immediately by direct pressure, wound packing or a tourniquet applied as distally as possible; no blind clamping; if unstable with uncontrolled bleeding, resuscitate and operate together. MoHFW 2025: stepwise — manual pressure, pressure dressing, occlude the proximal artery, manual tourniquet, then realign, reduce and immobilise. ICMR STW 2024: local pressure; if bleeding does not stop, pack the wound. Tourniquet technique: see Major trauma.' Change the BOAST_ARTERIAL locator to 'Standards 2–5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15; footnote ii' and add ICMR_OPENFX 'Initial emergency treatment — obvious bleed'.
issues.evidence: BOA Standard 'Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma' (June 2026), Standard 2: 'Haemorrhage must be controlled immediately by direct pressure, wound packing, or tourniquet applied as distally as possible. Blind clamping should not be undertaken.' Standard 3: 'Haemodynamically unstable patients with uncontrolled bleeding should undergo simultaneous emergency resuscitation and surgical intervention.' (https://www.boa.ac.uk/asset/7E8D1CA3-7448-47C7-84980C6D3E7E96B0/). MoHFW STG Trauma 2025, Ch. 10 Major Arterial Haemorrhage (p. 48): 'Stepwise scontrol (go to next step, if bleeding is not controlled) o Apply manual pressure to the wound o Put pressure dressing using a stack of gauze pads o Occlude the proximal artery o Apply a manual tourniquet o Realign the fractures, reduce the joints and immobilise'. ICMR STW Open Fractures 2024: 'OBVIOUS BLEED ... Apply local pressure ... Does not stop ... Pack the wound' (https://www.icmr.gov.in/icmrobject/uploads/STWs/1726645314_9_open_fracture.pdf).

issues.claim: StepDose("Gentamicin — Gustilo III (GAIS/WSES 2024; ICMR STW 2024)", WeightDose(5.0, 5.0, ...)); StepDose("Gentamicin — ED loading dose, adult (MoHFW 2025)", ...); StepDose("Gentamicin — ED loading dose, child or <50 kg (MoHFW 2025)", ...) — no renal, shock or crush caution anywhere in the protocol.
issues.problem: The protocol shows three gentamicin calculators with no warning. The cited sources warn about aminoglycosides in exactly the patients who get them: shocked, polytrauma and crush casualties. INSARAG 2023 says to avoid aminoglycosides in crush injury, and the sister Compartment syndrome and crush protocol repeats this. Crush victims after building collapse often have open fractures (Sever 2023), so the two protocols give conflicting instructions for the same patient. GAIS/WSES 2024 says to avoid aminoglycosides where possible and to adjust doses in haemorrhagic shock with AKI. The EAST 2011 article's invited commentary flags nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity with renal compromise, shock or contrast. ICMR 2019 bases aminoglycoside maintenance doses on creatinine clearance.
issues.correction: Add a point, and a note on each gentamicin StepDose: 'Gentamicin cautions — INSARAG 2023: avoid aminoglycosides in crush injury (see Compartment syndrome and crush injury). GAIS/WSES 2024: in haemorrhagic shock with AKI, adjust antibiotic doses. ICMR 2019: give the loading dose regardless of renal function; base maintenance on creatinine clearance.' Cite INSARAG ('§5 Medications — antibiotics'), ABX_2024 ('Abdominal trauma — rationale') and ICMR_AMR ('Ch. 14, Table 14.1 notes'). Add INSARAG to this protocol's citations.
issues.evidence: INSARAG MWG technical reference note 2023, §5 Medications: 'Antibiotics: ... consider administration of broad spectrum (including anaerobes) intravenous or intramuscular antibiotics (in non-damaged tissue); avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics (e.g. aminoglycosides).' and 'Patients presenting with possible acute renal failure may accumulate excessive doses of an administered drug due to inability of urinary excretion leading to toxicity.' (https://insarag.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Attachment-C2-MWG-The-Medical-Management-of-the-Entrapped-Patient-with-Crush-Syndrome-March-2023.pdf). GAIS/SIS-E/WSIS/AAST/WSES 2024 (J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2024;96(4):674–682), Abdominal trauma: 'aminoglycosides should be avoided whenever possible. In the case of hemorrhagic shock and associated acute kidney injury, the dose of antibiotics should be adjusted.' EAST 2011 (J Trauma 2011;70(3):751–754), invited commentary: 'The risks of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity with aminoglycosides are becoming more germane ... critically important if the patient has preexisting renal compromise or if the patient has impaired renal perfusion as a consequence of systemic shock.' ICMR AMR guidelines 2019, Ch. 14 Table 14.1 notes: 'the loading dose should be given to all patients regardless of the patient's creatinine clearance. Maintenance dose is based on the creatinine clearance'. Sever 2023 (Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc 57(6)): 'Earthquake-induced crush injuries are high-energy injuries. Therefore, open and comminuted fractures are common.'

issues.claim: AAOS 2025: neuraxial anaesthesia may complicate diagnosis — examine frequently and/or monitor pressure. BOAST 2025: regional anaesthesia by joint, documented decision.
issues.problem: The point leaves out what the cited sources actually say to do when regional anaesthesia is used in a limb at risk. The Association of Anaesthetists 2021 guideline's main recommendation is to avoid dense blocks of long duration that significantly exceed the duration of surgery, and to use lower concentrations without adjuncts with proper surveillance. BOAST 2025 Standard 6b requires an agreed policy for post-operative compartment monitoring, by invasive monitoring or review by trained staff. As written, the only BOAST content shown is a consent process, so a doctor in India giving a femoral or popliteal block, or a spinal, for a tibial fracture gets no instruction on block choice or monitoring. The Association of Anaesthetists 2021 is cited in this protocol but not for this point.
issues.correction: Replace with: 'Regional anaesthesia — Association of Anaesthetists 2021: avoid neuraxial or peripheral blocks that are dense and last well beyond surgery; lower-concentration blocks without adjuncts are not linked to delayed diagnosis if surveillance is in place. BOAST 2025: decide jointly (patient, anaesthetist, surgeon) and document; agree who monitors — invasive pressure monitoring or review by trained staff. AAOS 2025: after neuraxial anaesthesia, examine frequently and/or monitor pressure.' Add cite(AOA_ACS, "Recommendations; Pain relief after lower leg trauma") and extend the BOAST_CS locator to 'Standards 2–6 and footnote **'.
issues.evidence: Association of Anaesthetists 2021 (Nathanson MH et al., Anaesthesia 2021;76:1518–1525), Recommendations: 'The available literature suggests that the use of neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques that result in dense blocks of long duration, that is, significantly exceeding the duration of surgery, should be avoided.' and 'the use of single-shot or continuous peripheral nerve blocks using lower concentrations of local anaesthetic drugs without adjuncts are not associated with delays in diagnosis, provided appropriate post-injury and postoperative surveillance is used.' (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15504). BOAST 2025, Standard 6: 'The use of regional anaesthesia in extremity trauma: a. should follow joint decision making ... b. should have an agreed policy that includes responsibility for post operative monitoring for compartment syndrome**' with footnote '** Assessment should include either invasive monitoring or review by staff trained in regional anaesthesia and the assessment of compartment syndrome' (https://www.boa.ac.uk/asset/D0432D40-5D99-4B64-9952F6EB1B60C166/).

issues.step: Unstable pelvic fracture: packing, angioembolisation, REBOA
issues.claim: timing = "After binder, haemostatic resuscitation and exclusion of other bleeding sources (WSES 2017)"
issues.problem: WSES 2017 sets this prerequisite for angiography and angioembolisation only. The step's timing applies it to the whole step, including preperitoneal packing, which WSES says should 'always be considered' for pelvic-fracture instability. In MoHFW Fig. 12, packing comes together with laparotomy when FAST or DPL shows haemoperitoneum. Read as a gate, the timing could delay packing in a shocked patient at a centre without angiography, the setting where WSES favours packing most.
issues.correction: timing = "Binder and haemostatic resuscitation first; angioembolisation once extra-pelvic bleeding is excluded (WSES 2017)"
issues.evidence: WSES pelvic 2017 (World J Emerg Surg 2017;12:5), Role of angioembolization: 'After pelvic stabilization, initiation of aggressive hemostatic resuscitation and exclusion of extra-pelvic sources of blood loss, patients with pelvic fractures and hemodynamic instability or evidence of ongoing bleeding should be considered for pelvic angiography/angioembolization [Grade 2A].' Role of pre-peritoneal pelvic packing: 'Patients with pelvic fracture-related hemodynamic instability should always be considered for pre-peritoneal pelvic packing, especially in hospitals with no angiography service [Grade 1C].' https://doi.org/10.1186/s13017-017-0117-6

issues.step: eFAST, X-rays and DPL: role and limits (and note 'FAST differs')
issues.claim: cite(LA_EU, "R8") in the step's citations; note: "FAST differs: MoHFW 2025 makes eFAST mandatory for major trauma and for all yellow-area patients; NICE NG39 advises against FAST before immediate CT or as a screen for CT."
issues.problem: The step cites European 2023 R8 but no point is attributed to European 2023, so the citation supports nothing on screen. R8 is also a third position on FAST that the 'FAST differs' note omits: it recommends POCUS including FAST in thoracoabdominal injury (1C) and early contrast whole-body CT (1B). The released Major trauma protocol already reports this.
issues.correction: Add to the step: 'European 2023: POCUS including FAST in thoracoabdominal injury (1C); early contrast whole-body CT to find the bleeding source (1B).' Extend the note: '... European 2023 recommends POCUS including FAST in thoracoabdominal injury and early whole-body CT.' Add cite(LA_EU, "R8") to the note.
issues.evidence: European guideline 2023 (Crit Care 2023;27:80), Recommendation 8: 'We recommend the use of point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS), including FAST, in patients with thoracoabdominal injuries (Grade 1C). We recommend early imaging using contrast-enhanced whole-body CT (WBCT) for the detection and identification of the type of injury and the potential source of bleeding (Grade 1B).' https://doi.org/10.1186/s13054-023-04327-7

issues.claim: MoHFW 2025: an open long-bone or pelvic fracture is a red-triage criterion; manage ABCD first and immobilise life-threatening fractures in the primary survey.
issues.problem: The wording can be read as 'open (long-bone or pelvic) fracture', which limits red triage to open pelvic fractures. MoHFW lists any pelvic fracture as a red criterion, separately from open long-bone fractures; the released Major trauma checklist has 'Open long-bone fracture or pelvic fracture'. Under-triaging a closed pelvic fracture is a safety risk.
issues.correction: MoHFW 2025: open long-bone fractures and any pelvic fracture are red-triage criteria; manage ABCD first and immobilise life-threatening fractures in the primary survey.
issues.evidence: MoHFW STG Trauma 2025, Ch. 1 'Triage Criteria: RED category patients' (pp. 6–7): '4. Major crush injuries 5. Vascular injuries 6. Pregnancy 7. Open long bones fractures 8. Pelvic fracture' — https://www.dghs.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/assets/SwQ7pJMiJepMtqfUQNUJrGOROd584XHIgipqf7gI.pdf
